title: Beyond water transport: aquaporins mediate systemic ROS signaling to enhance stress resilience in rice roots
content: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst is a key signal relayed during biotic and abiotic stresses, including high salt and heavy metals (Cuypers et al 2010; Zhu 2016; Kolahi et al 2020; Wang et al 2023). In rice roots, both these stressors induce a local and rapid ROS burst, which is then propagated to systemic root tissues as part of adaptive responses (Wang et al 2023). The plasma membrane–localized intrinsic proteins (PIPs) or aquaporins actively transport hydrogen peroxide, a major form of ROS with implications for stress adaptations (Dynowski et al 2008; Bienert and Chaumont 2014; Zhang et al 2023). For example, the rice aquaporins OsPIP2;1 and OsPIP2;2 play an important role in alkaline stress adaptation by regulating redox homeostasis (Zhang et al 2023). However, the role of rice aquaporins in adaptation to salt and heavy metals such as cadmium (Cd) stress via ROS transport and propagation remains to be investigated. In this issue of Plant Physiology, Zhao et al (2026) addressed this gap and revealed a previously unrecognized role of aquaporins in systemic ROS signaling for heavy metal and salt stress adaptation in rice roots.
